Modern network switches use store-and-forward switching by default: the switch buffers
an entire Ethernet frame, checks its frame check sequence for errors, and only then
forwards it out the destination port. This trades a small amount of latency for
reliability, since a corrupted frame is dropped before it can consume bandwidth
downstream. Cut-through switching, by contrast, begins forwarding as soon as the
destination address is read from the frame header, reducing latency at the cost of
occasionally propagating a runt or corrupted frame.
